newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - Portugal's Cinderella city gets its reward.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Portugal's Cinderella city gets its reward.

text.p: OPORTO, Portugal, April 2 - Home of one of the world's most famous wines, Oporto has a new reason for cheer in its eternal rivalry with Portugal's capital, Lisbon.
The city's old centre, with its cobbled streets, thick stone houses, some dating back to the Middle Ages, and Baroque churches has been acclaimed one of the world's architectural jewels.

The United Nations Educational, Scientic and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO), in its 1996 role of honour, added part of Oporto to its list of World Heritage Sites, a designation reserved for places of "exceptional universal value."
For its people, not content with giving the world port wine or having arguably the country's most successful soccer team, UNESCO's recognition is a matter for deep satisfaction.
"It is a stimulus for Oporto's sense of individuality and civic pride. It has given us a great boost," said long-serving city mayor Fernando Gomes.
LONG IN THE CAPITAL'S SHADOW
Set at the mouth of the Douro river, whose steep-banked valley provides the unique soil conditions for the grapes used in the production of port, the northern city has long lived in Lisbon's shadow.

Some tourists may stop off on their way to Portugal's southerly beaches to visit the wine warehouses on the waterfront and admire the few old port barges bobbing gently on the tide -- a reminder of bygone days before wine was trucked down from the valleys.
But in keeping with its gritty and workmanlike image, most of the visitors to the port city come on business or to attend congresses or trade fairs.
One of immediate advantages of the UNESCO award, which carries no cash, has been a significant increase in the number of such bookings, Gomes told Reuters.

It should also keep up pressure for financing for restoration work, with some six billion escudos ($35 million) of projects, ranging from drainage to a luxury hotel, underway with the help of central government and the European Union.
REGARDS CAPITAL WITH DEEP DISTRUST
Like Italy's Milan or Barcelona in Spain, Oporto has traditionally seen itself as Portugal's industrial powerhouse, regarding the more southernly capital with deep distrust and some disdain.

"There is a popular saying that the north works and the south has fun...but it is just a saying and not really true," said Gomes. "The people in Lisbon know how to work and we know how to enjoy ourselves."

But there is no doubt that the UNESCO award comes at a welcome time, as pressure on its traditional industries and an unemployment rate higher than the national average were shaking the city's self-belief.

Port made one of the city's first fortunes and the warehouses still bear the names of British families -- Cockburns, Sandemans, Taylors -- even if most have long since been swallowed up by international drinks companies.

Port exporters continue to gather at their 18th century city club to wine and dine amid surroundings and customs that have made few concessions to the passing of time. Women cannot become members and can dine there only a couple of times a year.
The wine business is worth $400 million a year in exports but it has long been overtaken in importance by industries such as shoes, clothing and textiles.
INDUSTRY FELL ON HARD TIMES

However, economic recession in Europe in the early 1990s and rising competition from lower cost producers in the Far East has put its textile and clothes business under increasing pressure, boosting unemployment to over 11 percent against the national average of seven.

The sense of local grievance has been stoked by the perception that in recent years a disproportionate amount of state investment -- which can create jobs through infrastructure projects -- has been focused on the south around Lisbon.
Top of the list for complaint is the ambitious 1998 World Exhibition being held in Lisbon to mark the 500th anniversary of navigator Vasco da Gama's voyage of discovery to India.
"It is costing more than than Portugal received in funding from the European Union between 1989 and 1994," said Gomes.
The outstanding domestic success of soccer club Porto has proved a vehicle for the city's need to assert itself against the dominance of its old rival Lisbon.
When Porto crushed Lisbon's Benfica, once the country's most renowned team, 5-0 earlier this season, local wags began calling for the capital's telephone prefix to be changed to 05 from 01.
Now UNESCO has given the proud northerners another cause to smile.
